title: Start praying five times a day
whyMatters: Prayer (salah) is the most important thing a Muslim does in a day. It is a direct conversation with Allah. Five times a day you stop, put the noise down, and turn towards your Creator. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) called prayer the coolness of his eyes. Learning it can feel daunting at the start, but every Muslim you have met began at zero, and every prayer you offer counts with Allah even when it comes out rough.

subSteps: Fajr: before sunrise, usually the quietest one of the day.
Dhuhr: after the sun passes its peak, early afternoon.
Asr: late afternoon.
Maghrib: just after sunset.
Isha: at night, once the twilight has gone.
Download a prayer time app such as Muslim Pro or Athan to get accurate times for Toronto.
Wudu is the wash you do before prayer: hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, a wipe over the head, then the feet.
Each part is washed three times, and wiping the head is done once.
Make sure the water reaches everywhere it needs to.
Your wudu stays valid until something breaks it, such as using the bathroom, passing gas, sleeping, or bleeding heavily.
Al-Fatiha is the opening chapter of the Quran and it is recited in every unit (rak'ah) of prayer.
Start by reading the transliteration alongside the Arabic text.
Listen to a slow recitation and repeat it phrase by phrase.
Practice a few lines each day. Most people have it within one or two weeks.
Reading from paper or a phone screen while you learn is fine.
Standing (qiyam): recite Al-Fatiha and a short surah.
Bowing (ruku): bend at the waist with your hands on your knees and say 'Subhana Rabbiyal Adheem' (Glory to my Lord, the Most Great).
Prostration (sujud): forehead, nose, palms, knees, and toes on the ground, saying 'Subhana Rabbiyal A'la' (Glory to my Lord, the Most High).
Sitting (juloos): sit between the two prostrations.
These movements repeat to form one unit (rak'ah). Different prayers have different numbers of rak'at.

exactActions.text: Know the number of rak'at for each prayer
subSteps: Fajr: 2 rak'at.
Dhuhr: 4 rak'at.
Asr: 4 rak'at.
Maghrib: 3 rak'at.
Isha: 4 rak'at.
Start with the obligatory (fard) prayers. You can add the voluntary (sunnah) ones later.
Find a clean, quiet spot. Use a prayer mat or a clean towel.
Face the qiblah, the direction of the Ka'bah in Mecca. From Toronto that is roughly northeast.
Begin with the intention in your heart, raise your hands, and say 'Allahu Akbar' (God is Greatest).
Follow the movements you have learned. Glancing at a guide beside you is fine.
End by turning your head right and left, saying 'As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah' (Peace and mercy of Allah be upon you).

timeEstimate: 1 to 2 weeks to learn the basics, then daily practice

obstacles.problem: I can't memorize the Arabic words
obstacles.solution: This is normal. Arabic is a new language for most converts. Break Al-Fatiha into short phrases and take a line a day. Listen to recordings on your commute. Plenty of converts need weeks to hold the whole thing, and that is fine. In the meantime, recite what you have and make du'a in your own language for the rest. Allah sees the effort.

A five-times-a-day habit takes a while to build. Focus on one or two prayers first, and many people suggest Fajr and Maghrib. Set alarms for the times. If you miss one, pray it as soon as you remember instead of writing off the day. Every prayer you catch counts.

obstacles.problem: I don't know how many rak'at to pray
obstacles.solution: Keep a small card or a note on your phone. Fajr is 2, Dhuhr is 4, Asr is 4, Maghrib is 3, Isha is 4. It becomes automatic sooner than you expect. If you lose count mid-prayer, go with the lower number and add a prostration of forgetfulness (sujud al-sahw) at the end.

obstacles.problem: I can't pray at work or school
obstacles.solution: You have the right to pray. Muslims manage it in quiet corners, empty meeting rooms, and parked cars. A prayer takes five to ten minutes. If the timing is difficult, some prayers can be combined in certain situations, so ask a teacher about yours. Mention it to a colleague or supervisor if you feel comfortable, and most people turn out to be reasonable about it.

obstacles.problem: I feel self-conscious about the movements
obstacles.solution: Pray in private until it feels less exposed. Home is the best place to learn. When you are ready to pray at a masjid, follow the people around you. Nobody is grading your form, because everyone there is occupied with their own prayer.

tinyVersion: If it all feels like too much, start with one prayer a day. Standing, bowing, prostrating, and speaking to Allah from your heart counts, even in its plainest form. You can tidy up the details as you learn.
unlocksNext: Once prayer has a place in your day, you are ready to find your local Muslim community, the people who will walk this road with you.
